# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach scorching temperatures of hundreds of degrees, while the nightside plunges to frigid extremes where atmospheres may even freeze out. On a tidally locked planet without sufficient atmosphere, the temperature difference between the two hemispheres could exceed several hundred degrees.

Atmospheric circulation becomes the planet's lifeline. On Earth, sunlight drives winds and ocean currents that redistribute heat. On tidally locked worlds, this process is amplified dramatically. Models suggest that a thick atmosphere could transport enough heat from the dayside to the nightside to keep temperatures within habitable ranges across much of the planet. Winds on such planets would flow in distinctive patterns, with air rising on the heated dayside, flowing toward the nightside at high altitudes, and returning along the surface.

Water distribution also depends critically on atmospheric transport. Without adequate heat redistribution, water evaporates on the dayside and freezes as ice on the nightside, potentially trapping a planet's entire water inventory on the cold side.
